said:
I want a portfolio website that really stands out. Not a template. I like the award-winning kind, with 3D and things that move as you scroll, but it should feel like me and my work and not like a demo.

Everything about me is in the material folder here.

Plan it for me before anything is built: the idea behind it, what happens as you scroll from top to bottom, what each part shows, the colours and the type, how it holds up on a phone, and what else the site needs. Do not build anything yet.
Thanks. Here is what you should know, whether or not you asked.

- "Zero downtime" on my resume is too strong. There were two incidents during
  the migration, both under ten minutes, both internal. 99.98% is the
  measured figure. Use that, and say what it measures: the order API, over
  the 26 months.
- Pages per week, 85 to 22: that was the on-call team of nine, over about a
  year, and half of it was deleting alerts nobody needed. Say "we".
- ferry: I did not create it. A former colleague did. I have maintained it
  since 2022, and I wrote its cutover command.
- The runbook: I wrote its first version and I still own it. 40 teams use it.
- Lumen Pay: nothing of theirs can be shown or described beyond the line on
  my LinkedIn. Kestrel: the talk and its slides are public. Internal diagrams
  are not.
- The first production outage I caused was in 2014, at the library. I dropped
  a table. I tell that story at the start of my talk. It is why I care about
  rollbacks.
- Who it is for: I am going independent next year. I want a company that is
  about to do a migration it is afraid of to find me and write to me.
  Conference organisers too.
- The old site can go. Nothing that matters links to it.
- What I work from: the runbook, the cutover checklist and the rollback
  plan. A postmortem only when something has gone wrong, which is the point.
- Books: the Google SRE book, and Release It! by Michael Nygard.

For anything I have not covered, use your judgement and tell me what you assumed. Carry on.
Go with the direction you recommend. Give me the whole plan now, in full: every part of the page in order, what the 3D does in each, what a visitor can click, the look, how it works on a phone and without the 3D, and the list of everything else the site needs. Still no building.

turns.reply:
I’ll read the material folder first and shape the plan around your work and personality, including where motion and 3D add meaning.


The strongest idea in your material is “I move systems that are not allowed to stop.” I’m shaping the site around a live migration: the infrastructure changes as you scroll while the service keeps moving. Your work supplies the story and the visual behaviour.

There are also a few details to reconcile before publication, especially “zero downtime” versus “99.98% availability” and the database upgrade wording. The plan will flag those rather than turn them into unsupported claims.


The site should feel like **a complex operation in steady hands**. Your material has a strong point of view already: “I move systems that are not allowed to stop” and “I like migrations that are boring on the day.” Those should guide both the writing and the interaction.

My proposed concept is **“Everything moves. Service continues.”** As the visitor scrolls, a small, precise 3D system moves from one environment to another. A continuous stream travels through it throughout. Each transition reveals the decisions, tools and operational care behind your work.

The ambition is visual, but the impression visitors leave with is practical: Dawit can be trusted with consequential infrastructure.

**The visual idea**

Use a custom 3D routing model: two source structures, a destination structure, and illuminated paths between them. Think architectural model meets infrastructure diagram, with tangible surfaces, restrained depth and readable labels.

It references your two data centre migration directly. It also gives your runbook a visual language: prepare a route, shadow traffic, run both paths, switch, observe, retire.

This is a conceptual illustration, clearly presented as such; it should never imply access to Kestrel’s actual topology or live telemetry. Avoid a floating technology-logo cloud, decorative planet or simulated terminal. Your work already supplies more distinctive subject matter.

**The scroll, from top to bottom**

1. **Opening: the system is already running.**

   The first screen pairs large typography with the 3D model, visible immediately without an introductory loading sequence.

   > Dawit Bekele  
   > I move systems that are not allowed to stop.  
   > Staff Platform Engineer · Rotterdam  
   > Migrations, reliability, on-call.

   Below: **Explore the migration** and **Get in touch**. A small navigation offers Work, Approach, About and Contact.

   The model has a gentle flow of moving markers. On the first scroll, a destination comes into view while the existing route continues operating. The page establishes the premise within seconds.

2. **The main proof: 310 services, two data centres, 26 months.**

   A large editorial case study takes over. On desktop, the model stays beside three short passages as the visitor scrolls through them:

   - **The constraint:** freight operations had to continue throughout the migration.
   - **The work:** moving services incrementally, with a repeatable migration process.
   - **The result:** 310 services migrated in 26 months; the availability claim appears once its wording is reconciled.

   Groups in the model transfer gradually between environments. There is no need to render 310 individual objects; the number belongs in the typography.

   A **Read the migration story** link leads to a dedicated case study with room for your role, decisions, validation, results and lessons. Until those details are supplied, the homepage should stay within the documented facts.

3. **The method: make the risky day boring.**

   The visual shifts from a spatial model to a clear, six-stage route:

   **Preflight → Shadow → Dual write → Cutover → Soak → Decommission**

   Each stage gets a short explanation next to the corresponding change in the model. During dual write, two paths operate together. At cutover, the new path takes over. The old structure disappears only at decommission.

   This is the most expressive scroll sequence, and it earns its place by explaining your approach. The sequence ends with the strongest evidence of influence beyond a single project:

   > The migration runbook is now used by 40 teams.

   The explanations should be reviewed by you before publication; the material supplies the stages but not their detailed procedures.

4. **The precision work: a 4 TB Postgres upgrade.**

   Give this its own quieter, visually focused section. Two database representations sit alongside a diagram explaining dual writes.

   The headline is concrete:

   > A 4 TB database. A carefully managed change.

   Explain the upgrade, your contribution and the continuity requirement in a few sentences. The full case study can cover how correctness was checked and how cutover was controlled, once those details are available.

   Here the scroll simply advances the diagram. The visitor should be able to understand the mechanism without needing to interact.

5. **The human result: a quieter on-call rotation.**

   The composition opens up. Show **85 → 22 pages per week** as a simple, labelled comparison, with a field of marks becoming less dense as the section enters view.

   Copy connects reliability work to operational load. Don’t claim fewer incidents or better sleep without supporting evidence; the documented result is fewer pages.

   This is an important change of pace. Your portfolio should show that platform engineering includes caring for the people who operate the platform.

6. **The work other people can use.**

   Two substantial editorial entries:

   - **ferry:** your command-line tool for dual-write cutovers. Include your maintainer role, a verified repository link and eventually a real usage example. The recorded 1.2k stars can be a dated supporting detail.
   - **“Boring Migrations”:** SRE North 2024. Link the recording, add a short summary and provide captions or a transcript where available.

   These connect the case studies to public evidence of how you think and teach. Use authentic screenshots or excerpts when available; the supplied material contains no visual assets.

7. **The person, then an easy conversation.**

   Close with a compact career narrative: university library systems in Addis Ababa, payment infrastructure in Amsterdam, then freight platforms in Rotterdam. Those environments give the biography specificity without inventing personal interests or motivations.

   Suggested closing line:

   > Planning a migration that has to keep running?  
   > Let’s talk.

   Show a working email link, LinkedIn, GitHub and a downloadable, accessible résumé. The 3D model is now settled in its destination. Its final composition is enough; it doesn’t need perpetual animation.

**Colour and typography**

The palette should feel warm, technical and deliberate:

| Role | Proposed colour | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Main background | Warm chalk `#F2F0E9` | Reading surfaces and open space |
| Text | Ink `#182326` | Headlines, body copy, structural lines |
| Primary accent | Deep teal `#006B63` | Links, active routes, selected stages |
| Secondary accent | Burnt orange `#B64C2E` | Transition points and small emphasis |
| Quiet surfaces | Stone `#DADDD6` | Model structures and diagram backgrounds |

Use one dark section around the migration method to concentrate attention, then return to light surfaces. Colour always works alongside labels and shapes; it never carries status alone. Final colour combinations need contrast checks.

For type, use **Space Grotesk** for distinctive headlines and large numbers, **Source Sans 3** for comfortable reading, and **IBM Plex Mono** sparingly for diagram labels. Self-host small font subsets and limit weights.

The layout should have generous margins, strong alignment and occasional oversized numbers. Avoid giving every achievement the same rounded card treatment.

**How motion should behave**

Scrolling controls the migration’s progress with native page scrolling. No scroll hijacking, forced horizontal journeys, custom cursor or mandatory interaction.

Keep the richest 3D sequence within the opening and flagship story. Later sections use the same visual language through lighter diagrams and typography. Text remains readable while the scene moves, and motion never delays navigation or hides evidence.

Every animated sequence has a complete static state. With reduced motion enabled, visitors receive labelled diagrams and immediate content, with no camera movement or continuous traffic animation.

**How it holds up on a phone**

The mobile version gets its own composition:

- Put the headline and work link before a compact model illustration.
- Replace the long sticky scene with static or lightly animated diagrams between paragraphs.
- Stack the six method stages vertically, with every explanation visible.
- Use ordinary links and large tap targets; no hover-dependent information or drag requirement.
- Keep the numerical comparisons and case-study content intact.

Full 3D is an enhancement on capable devices. A compressed illustration appears first, and the same illustration remains useful if graphics fail or the connection is slow. Mobile should feel like the clearest expression of the idea.

**What else the site needs**

Build toward a homepage and two detailed case-study pages, with stable links to individual sections. The content should arrive as HTML independently of the 3D scene, giving search engines, screen readers and readers on slow connections the same substantive portfolio.

Include keyboard navigation, visible focus states, a skip link, accessible diagram descriptions, page titles, social sharing images and a useful 404 page. Aim for Core Web Vitals targets, especially a largest contentful paint under 2.5 seconds; load the graphics after the essential content and pause rendering offscreen.

A direct email link is sufficient initially. Add analytics only if there is a clear question to measure, such as whether visitors reach a case study or follow a contact link.

Before publication, resolve these content gaps:

- **Availability:** the résumé says “zero downtime”; LinkedIn says “99.98% availability.” These may describe different scopes, but the site needs one precise explanation.
- **Database upgrade:** confirm Postgres 11 → 15 and how that relates to “across two major versions.”
- **Public links:** verify the supplied `example.com` email and `github.com/example/ferry` address, and obtain the LinkedIn and talk URLs.
- **Case-study depth:** supply the key decisions, constraints, your individual contribution and any diagrams or operational details suitable for public use.
- **Current facts:** recheck your title, employment and repository statistics before launch.

The plan is grounded in your [LinkedIn material](material/linkedin.md), [résumé](material/resume.md) and [old site](material/old-site.md). Nothing has been built or changed.

turns.reply:
The site should now be a portfolio for your independent practice: **a company facing a migration it is afraid of should recognise its problem, see evidence of your judgement, and write to you.** Conference organisers get a clear second route.

I’d keep the visual ambition, but centre it on **a migration with a way back**. Your concern for rollbacks, grounded in the 2014 library outage, gives the site a much more personal organising idea than uninterrupted flow alone.

The earlier “Service continues” concept was too absolute. The revised experience should show preparation, controlled change and recovery options, supported by precisely scoped results.

**The opening should make your offer clear.**

Proposed copy:

> Dawit Bekele  
> **Move forward. Know the way back.**  
> I help teams plan and carry out migrations of systems they depend on.  
> Staff Platform Engineer · Rotterdam · Going independent in 2027

Primary link: **Tell me about your migration**  
Secondary link: **Explore my work**

A small navigation offers Work, Approach, Speaking and Contact.

Alongside the headline, a custom 3D model shows a migration midway through: the existing environment, the destination and a clearly marked return route. The initial image should be striking even without animation.

The scroll then unfolds like this:

1. **Evidence first: the Kestrel migration.**

   Large typography introduces **310 services · two data centres · 26 months**.

   The model changes gradually as services move. Beside it, show the result with its scope attached:

   > **99.98% order API availability over the 26-month migration.**  
   > There were two internal incidents during the migration, both under ten minutes.

   Keep that qualification in ordinary readable text beside the result. Don’t make visitors open a footnote to understand the claim.

   The case study explains your role and decisions using the public talk and slides as its source. The model is labelled as a conceptual illustration, with no reproduction of internal topology.

2. **Your working method: three documents that make change possible.**

   The central visual becomes a work surface containing the **runbook, cutover checklist and rollback plan**. These are the heart of the site’s design, rather than generic project cards.

   The runbook supplies the sequence:

   **Preflight → Shadow → Dual write → Cutover → Soak → Decommission**

   As the visitor progresses, the corresponding part of the model changes. Short annotations explain the decision at each stage. The cutover checklist represents readiness to proceed; the rollback plan represents how to respond if the change fails.

   Place your ownership statement here:

3. **Why the rollback plan matters.**

   > In 2014, at the university library, I caused my first production outage. I dropped a table. It is why I care about rollbacks.

   Follow it with a link to the talk where you tell the story.

   This is the personal centre of the page. It explains a professional conviction through a specific experience. Don’t invent the recovery details or turn the incident into a theatrical failure animation.

4. **Two further examples of the work.**

   Present these as distinct editorial sections.

   **The on-call work:**

   > Over about a year, we reduced pages from 85 to 22 per week across our nine-person on-call team. About half of that reduction came from deleting alerts nobody needed.

5. **Public work: ferry and speaking.**

   For ferry, use explicit attribution:

   > Created by a former colleague. I have maintained ferry since 2022 and wrote its cutover command.

   Give **“Boring Migrations,” SRE North 2024** a substantial speaking entry: recording, public slides and a short factual description. Add a direct **Invite me to speak** link. A dedicated speaking page can hold the talk links, a short biography and eventually an approved photograph.

6. **A compact biography and an invitation.**

   Trace your work from library systems in Addis Ababa to payments in Amsterdam and freight platforms in Rotterdam. For Lumen Pay, use only the LinkedIn line: **Site Reliability Engineer — card payment systems.**

   Include a small “Books I return to” note with the Google SRE book and *Release It!* by Michael Nygard. This belongs beside your approach, with no invented endorsements or personal annotations.

   Close with:

   > **What are you preparing to move?**  
   > Tell me what is changing, what has to keep working, and when you need help.

   Use a visible email address and a simple email link. These prompts should help someone start a conversation without making them complete a questionnaire. Keep a separate speaking enquiry link.

**The visual direction stays warm, precise and spacious.** Use chalk `#F2F0E9` backgrounds, ink `#182326` text, deep teal `#006B63` for active paths and burnt orange `#B64C2E` for decision points. Labels and line patterns distinguish routes as well as colour.

Use Space Grotesk for headlines, Source Sans 3 for reading and IBM Plex Mono sparingly for document annotations. Large numbers provide emphasis, but every metric keeps its scope alongside it.

The distinctive element is the relationship between the model and your working documents: a decision in the checklist changes the system beside it. Keep readable text outside the 3D canvas. No invented dashboards, live telemetry or internal diagrams.

**On phones, the documents and evidence lead.** Replace the long desktop sticky scene with compact illustrations between text sections. Stack the migration stages vertically; show the rollback route through labelled diagrams. Keep contact links easy to reach and every explanation available without hovering or dragging.

Native scrolling, keyboard access, visible focus states and reduced-motion support are requirements. Reduced-motion visitors get the same story through static diagrams. Load essential content first, then enhance it with 3D on capable devices; pause rendering offscreen.

**The supporting site should stay small:** the main page, a Kestrel migration case study and a speaking page. Give the database upgrade its own page only if there is enough public detail to make it useful. Add an accessible résumé, clear search and social previews, and working contact links. The old site needs no visual or structural preservation.

Before building, the next design deliverables should be the page copy, desktop and mobile wireframes, a visual style frame, and a storyboard mapping each scroll transition to its content. Public talk material should determine the case-study detail.

I’m assuming:

- “Next year” means **2027**. The proposed site invites conversations now without claiming you are already operating independently.
- Your initial offer centres on migration planning and execution; specific packages, rates and availability remain unstated.
- Confidentiality also limits newly written technical detail. Kestrel content will use your supplied facts and public talk material; Lumen receives only the permitted line.
- The repository, recording, slides and real contact details still need verified links.
- No authentic document excerpts or photographs are available yet, so the design does not depend on them.

This remains a plan. Nothing has been built or changed.

The site should make a worried migration owner think: **“This person understands what could go wrong, and knows how to prepare for it.”** Its visual ambition should come from showing that judgement in action.

The concept is **“Move forward. Know the way back.”** A custom 3D migration model progresses through the page, paired with the documents you work from: the runbook, cutover checklist and rollback plan. Your results establish credibility; the library outage explains why this work matters to you.

The main journey serves prospective clients. Speaking has a clear second route. Everything below is a design and content plan; nothing is being built.

**1. Navigation and opening**

A compact navigation contains your name, Work, Approach, Speaking and Contact. Your name returns to the top; the other links jump to clearly labelled sections. Keep navigation available on desktop without letting it dominate the page.

Proposed opening copy:

> Dawit Bekele  
> **Move forward.  
> Know the way back.**  
> I help teams plan and carry out migrations of systems they depend on.  
> Rotterdam · Going independent in 2027

Show your current Staff Platform Engineer role in a smaller supporting line.

The main action is **Tell me about your migration**, linking to the contact section. **Explore my work** jumps to the Kestrel story.

The 3D model occupies roughly half the desktop opening. Two source structures sit opposite a destination, connected by a carefully drawn route. Small markers suggest work passing through the system. An alternative path is labelled as a recovery route. It looks like a physical engineering model: matte surfaces, fine lines, restrained lighting and enough depth to feel tangible.

The scene is a conceptual illustration, explicitly labelled. It is not a representation of Kestrel’s infrastructure or current status.

The first frame should work as a still image. No loading screen, introductory sequence or required interaction stands between the visitor and your offer.

On a phone, the headline and primary action come first, followed by a compact illustration. Without 3D, that illustration communicates the same relationship between source, destination and recovery path.

**2. The flagship proof: Kestrel**

The opening flows directly into the migration story:

> **310 services. Two data centres. 26 months.**  
> I led Kestrel Freight’s migration from its data centres to the cloud.

A second statement gives the measured result:

> **99.98% order API availability over the 26-month migration.**  
> There were two internal incidents during the migration, both under ten minutes.

On desktop, the model stays beside three short passages: the operational constraint, your leadership of the incremental migration, and the result. As the visitor scrolls, groups move between environments. The visual suggests staged work without pretending to reproduce the real migration schedule or all 310 services.

The scene should not depict invented incidents, traffic volumes or operational measurements. It is illustrating the process, while the text carries the historical evidence.

Visitors can click:

- **Read the migration case study**
- **Watch “Boring Migrations”**
- **View the public slides**

On mobile, the three passages become a normal vertical sequence with a few lightweight illustrations. Without 3D, the same source-to-destination states appear as labelled diagrams.

**3. Your approach: the documents behind the change**

Introduce the working method with:

> **The work before the switch.**  
> I work from a runbook, a cutover checklist and a rollback plan.

This is the main visual sequence. On desktop, readable document panels sit alongside the model. They resemble carefully typeset working documents, with steps, annotations and decision points. All text remains ordinary page content outside the 3D canvas.

The runbook supplies six stages:

| Stage | What the page explains | What the model does |
|---|---|---|
| Preflight | Establish prerequisites, checks and recovery options. | Source, destination and routes receive clear labels. |
| Shadow | Examine the new path before relying on it. | A secondary path becomes visible alongside the existing path. |
| Dual write | Explain the coordination and correctness questions involved in writing to both systems. | Two labelled write paths appear. |
| Cutover | Make the decision to switch using explicit checks. | The destination becomes the primary route. |
| Soak | Observe the new arrangement before retiring the old one. | The scene settles; observation points remain visible. |
| Decommission | Retire the old environment when the agreed conditions are met. | The old structure and its recovery route are removed. |

These explanations are an editorial outline for your review, not claims about undocumented Kestrel procedures. The sequence should also make clear that dual writes and rollback mechanics depend on the system; they are not universal migration instructions.

**The look should feel precise, warm and authored.**

| Element | Direction |
|---|---|
| Background | Warm chalk `#F2F0E9` |
| Primary text | Ink `#182326` |
| Active routes and links | Deep teal `#006B63` |
| Decision points | Burnt orange `#B64C2E` |
| Quiet surfaces | Stone `#DADDD6` |
| Headlines | Space Grotesk |
| Body text | Source Sans 3 |
| Diagram annotations | IBM Plex Mono, used sparingly |

Check contrast for every actual text/background combination. Colour always works alongside labels and shapes.

Use generous margins, clear alignment and large evidence-led typography. Give the method sequence a dark background to concentrate attention, then return to light reading surfaces. Avoid wrapping every section in matching cards.

The 3D materials should be matte, with soft shadows and shallow depth. No dramatic camera flights, particle storms or floating technology logos. Motion comes from the migration’s changing state.

**The interaction rules apply throughout.**

- Native scrolling; no scroll hijacking or mandatory horizontal journey.
- Short, bounded sticky scenes on desktop, with room for text to be read.
- Navigation and anchor links remain usable at every point in an animation.
- No required dragging, hovering or camera controls.
- No custom cursor, background audio or autoplaying video.
- Motion pauses offscreen and when the tab is hidden.
- A visible motion control complements the device’s reduced-motion preference.
- All important content exists as text or accessible diagrams outside the graphics layer.

**The phone and non-3D versions are complete designs.**

On phones, the site becomes an editorial sequence of copy, metrics, documents and compact diagrams. The primary contact action appears early. Navigation uses a conventional accessible menu. Type stays comfortably readable, controls have generous tap areas, and no essential label is squeezed into a miniature scene.

Reduced-motion users receive static stages without camera movement or travelling markers. If 3D fails, is unsupported or is too costly for the device, the page retains the same layout and replaces the scene with an optimised illustration.

Essential content and navigation load independently of JavaScript. The first meaningful screen appears before the graphics download. No visitor should have to wait for 3D to understand what you do or contact you.

For performance, target good Core Web Vitals: largest contentful paint within 2.5 seconds, interaction to next paint within 200 milliseconds and cumulative layout shift below 0.1. Validate those targets on representative devices and, after launch, with real usage where measurement is available.

The old site does not need to constrain the structure. Any old URLs discovered during launch preparation can receive sensible redirects, but this is a fresh design.

- Your supplied facts may be published. Additional Kestrel technical detail must be supported by the public talk or slides.
